question.prompt: A set of \(n\) people participate in an online video basketball tournament. Each person may be a member of any number of \(5\)-player teams, but no two teams may have exactly the same \(5\) members. The site statistics show a curious fact: The average, over all subsets of size \(9\) of the set of \(n\) participants, of the number of complete teams whose members are among those \(9\) people is equal to the reciprocal of the average, over all subsets of size \(8\) of the set of \(n\) participants, of the number of complete teams whose members are among those \(8\) people. How many values \(n,\) \(9 \le n \le 2017,\) can be the number of participants?

solutions.title: Count incidences, then allowed residues
solutions.explanation:
The key observation is that every fixed team belongs to the same number of subsets of a given size. This lets us compute the two averages using only the total number of teams.

Let \(T>0\) be the number of teams, and let \(M_k\) be the average number of complete teams in a \(k\)-person subset. A fixed team belongs to exactly \(\binom{n-5}{k-5}\) such subsets, since its five players are already chosen. Counting pairs consisting of a team and a subset containing it gives
\[
M_k=\frac{T\binom{n-5}{k-5}}{\binom nk}
=T\frac{\binom k5}{\binom n5}.
\]
In particular,
\[
M_9=\frac{126T}{\binom n5},\qquad
M_8=\frac{56T}{\binom n5}.
\]
The reciprocal condition says \(M_9M_8=1\). Since \(126\cdot56=84^2\), it follows that
\[
T=\frac{\binom n5}{84}
=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)(n-4)}{2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7}.
\]
For \(n\ge9\), this condition is also sufficient whenever \(T\) is an integer: it lies between \(1\) and \(\binom n5\), so we can choose that many distinct teams, and the computed averages have product one.

Set
\[
N=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)(n-4).
\]
We must count when \(N\) is divisible by \(32\cdot9\cdot5\cdot7\). Five consecutive integers always include a multiple of \(5\), so that factor imposes no restriction.

For divisibility by \(7\), the five factors must include a multiple of \(7\). This occurs exactly when
\[
n\equiv0,1,2,3,4\pmod7.
\]

For divisibility by \(9\), a multiple of \(9\) occurs when \(n\equiv0,1,2,3,4\pmod9\). The residues \(6,7\) also work because the five factors then include two multiples of \(3\). For residues \(5,8\), there is just one multiple of \(3\), and it is not divisible by \(9\). Thus the allowed residues are
\[
n\equiv0,1,2,3,4,6,7\pmod9.
\]

For divisibility by \(32=2^5\), count the factors of \(2\) supplied by the even terms:

- If \(n\) is odd, the even terms are \(n-1,n-3\). One has exactly one factor of \(2\), so the other must be divisible by \(16\). This gives \(n\equiv1,3\pmod{16}\).
- If \(n\equiv0\pmod4\), then \(n,n-4\) are both divisible by \(4\), and \(n-2\) is even. Together they supply at least five factors of \(2\), so all these values work.
- If \(n\equiv2\pmod4\), then \(n,n-4\) each supply exactly one factor of \(2\). Therefore \(n-2\) must be divisible by \(8\), giving \(n\equiv2,10\pmod{16}\).

Combining these cases, the eight allowed residues are
\[
n\equiv0,1,2,3,4,8,10,12\pmod{16}.
\]

The moduli \(7,9,16\) are pairwise coprime. By the Chinese remainder theorem, each choice of one allowed residue for each modulus determines exactly one residue modulo
\[
7\cdot9\cdot16=1008.
\]
Consequently, each block of \(1008\) consecutive integers contains exactly
\[
5\cdot7\cdot8=280
\]
solutions to the divisibility conditions.

The interval \(1\le n\le2016\) contains two complete blocks, giving \(560\) solutions. Among \(1,2,\ldots,8\), exactly \(1,2,3,4\) satisfy the residue conditions, so remove these four. Finally, \(2017\equiv1\pmod{1008}\) satisfies all three conditions and contributes one more value. The requested count is
\[
560-4+1=\boxed{557}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
